routes.description: Establish the relevant historical facts and show that divine resurrection explains them better than the principal skeptical alternatives within an appropriate theistic context.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical premises are sufficiently supported and resurrection provides the strongest comparative explanation without being excluded by an improper evidential standard or prior.

motionBridge.description: The historical evidence must make Jesus's resurrection the best explanation of the relevant facts.

centralBridges.description: The crucifixion, burial, empty tomb, postmortem experiences, and transformed disciples must be sufficiently established.
Resurrection must explain the established facts more adequately than conspiracy, hallucination, legendary development, and comparable skeptical alternatives.
The resurrection hypothesis must remain antecedently eligible for comparison when considered within an independently supported theistic context.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Historical proof must permit probabilistic inference to the best explanation rather than require mathematical demonstration.
Early and independent traditions must support the core reports despite differences among the completed Gospel narratives.

routes.description: Show that evidential standards, unfavorable prior probability, unreliable underlying reports, or viable naturalistic accounts prevent resurrection from becoming the best historical explanation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical data are insufficiently secure or resurrection remains less credible than skeptical alternatives after evidential standards and prior probabilities are incorporated.

motionBridge.description: Skeptical alternatives or evidential caution must prevent the historical record from warranting resurrection as the best explanation.

centralBridges.description: The exceptional supernatural and moral content of the claim must require evidence adequate to its asserted significance.
The exceptionally unfavorable prior probability of divine resurrection must be incorporated into comparison with naturalistic explanations.
The reliability, independence, and developmental history of the appearance reports must be tested before treating them as explanatory data.
Sincere mistake, hallucination, legendary development, or other naturalistic accounts must remain live comparative explanations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Historical facts surrounding the claim must be distinguished from the further inference that a resurrection occurred.
The quantity and clarity of the evidence must be assessed against the claim that God strongly desires human belief.

sectionSelections.title: Empirical Defeaters and Historical Inference
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue fixes whether religious warrant remains answerable to contrary public facts and distinguishes historical evidence for surrounding facts from the explanatory resurrection conclusion.

proSelections.proposition: Conclusive identification of Jesus's remains would falsify the resurrection, although archaeological uncertainty makes that scenario unlikely and the actual historical evidence is asserted to support resurrection.

conSelections.proposition: Decisive empirical evidence against the resurrection, such as authenticated remains of Jesus, would defeat contrary warrant attributed to religious experience.
Historical inquiry can establish facts surrounding the alleged resurrection, but resurrection itself remains a further inference to the best explanation.

sectionSelections.title: Historical Proof and Evidential Standards
sectionSelections.rationale: The applicable standard determines what degree and kind of historical support can warrant an extraordinary and uniquely consequential resurrection conclusion.

proSelections.proposition: Establishing resurrection as the most probable historical explanation constitutes proof in the ordinary probabilistic sense, though not mathematical demonstration.
Ordinary evidence can establish an extraordinary event when that evidence is much more probable if the event occurred than if it did not.

conSelections.proposition: The extraordinary nature, moral importance, and asserted divine purpose of resurrection justify demanding substantially stronger evidence than ordinary historical claims require.

sectionSelections.title: Divine Intent and Expected Evidence
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue connects the claimed divine authorship and importance of resurrection with the amount of evidence that should be expected and the standard applied to it.

proSelections.proposition: Resurrection should face the same epistemic historical standard as other events, even though Christianity's potential benefits may separately provide pragmatic reasons for belief.

conSelections.proposition: A God who strongly wants humanity to believe in resurrection should provide more evidence than the roughly ordinary historical record that appears available.

sectionSelections.title: Prior Probability and Theistic Context
sectionSelections.rationale: Comparative explanatory force depends on whether divine resurrection begins with an exceptionally unfavorable prior or becomes plausible within an independently supported theistic framework.

proSelections.proposition: Miracles are not intrinsically implausible if God exists, so resurrection evidence should be assessed within the theistic context supplied by independent arguments for a creator.

conSelections.proposition: Even weak naturalistic alternatives may remain more credible to an atheist because divine intervention raising a dead person has an exceptionally unfavorable prior probability.

sectionSelections.title: Historical Facts and Source Reliability
sectionSelections.rationale: The explanatory comparison can proceed only after determining whether the empty tomb, postmortem experiences, and related reports are sufficiently early, independent, and reliable.

proSelections.proposition: Five historical claims—crucifixion, burial, empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and transformed disciples—are presented as widely accepted facts best explained by resurrection under standard explanatory criteria.
Postmortem experiences are supported by early Pauline tradition, multiple Gospel attestations, and Mark's foreshadowing of appearances, while the core resurrection data are broadly accepted.

conSelections.proposition: Sparse and uneven attestation of group appearances, together with the earliest Gospel's lack of a narrated post-resurrection appearance, weakens confidence in the facts requiring explanation.
The progression from Mark's prediction through Matthew's doubted appearance to increasingly numerous later episodes supports suspicion of legendary development.

sectionSelections.title: Conspiracy, Hallucination, and Explanatory Scope
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue tests whether principal naturalistic accounts can explain sincere disciple belief, Jewish resurrection claims, reported appearances, and the empty tomb with adequate scope and power.

proSelections.proposition: Conspiracy is implausible because the earliest disciples sincerely endured suffering and would not have invented an isolated resurrection contrary to first-century Jewish expectations.
Hallucination lacks explanatory power because Jewish expectations would suggest Jesus in heaven rather than individually resurrected, and lacks scope because it does not explain the empty tomb.

conSelections.proposition: The disciples could sincerely die for a mistaken belief, with grief-induced hallucination providing a natural explanation for their conviction that Jesus had risen.
Chronologically later Gospel narratives contain increasingly elaborate appearance accounts, providing a natural source-development explanation for the resurrection tradition.
